description: All are welcome to attend the 19th Annual UCSF Health Equity and Anti-Racism Research (HEAR) Symposium taking place on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, 8 AM – 3:30 PM, at Mission Bay Conference Center. Register is free. tiny.ucsf.edu/HEAR. This year’s keynote speaker will be Olveen Carrasquillo, MD, MPH. Dr. Carrasquillo serves as Associate Dean of Clinical and Translational Research, Co-Director of the Clinical and Translational Science Center Institute, and Professor of Medicine and Public Health Sciences at University of Miami Miller School of Medicine. His advisory roles include the NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood (NHLBI) Advisory Council; chair of Patient Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI) Clinical Trails Advisory Panel, and chair of the Journal of General Internal Medicine editorial board. Dr. Carrasquillo holds over 25 years leading NIH-funded clinical, community-based health, and multi-center research projects, including as Multiple Principal Investigator (MPI) for the NIH All of Us program. HEAR Symposium offers AI-enabled live translation in 10 languages – smartphone or tablet required. UCSF welcomes all participants to our events. If you need to request a reasonable accommodation to participate in our event due to a disability, please contact Brooks Bigart by emailing brooksley.bigart@ucsf.edu as soon as possible. description: The ancestral recombination graph (ARG) is a structure that represents the history of coalescent and recombination events connecting a set of genomic sequences. The study of the ARG can yield valuable insights about past evolutionary processes. The ARG contains as much information about evolutionary processes, if not more, than the combination of all independent summary statistics that could be derived from genotypes. Consistent with this idea, some of the first ARG-based analyses to infer the past have proven to be more powerful than analyses that do not employ the ARG. Here I will present three projects that use the ARG to study the action of natural selection. First, I will present a new method to estimate the distribution of fitness effects of new mutations using the ARG. I show that our method provides better estimates of the distribution of fitness effects on some demographic scenarios compared to methods that do not use the ARG. Second, I present a methodology to infer the mutational model of STRs employing the ARG. I show that the method can estimate the mutation rate of STRs as well as parameters that determine the dynamics of changes in the number of STR motifs due to a single mutation. I present ideas on how we could use this method to study the distribution of fitness effects acting on STRs. Finally, I present a method that employs the ARG to estimate the strength of stabilizing selection acting on a complex trait.

description: Join UCSF researchers for a practical look at new generative AI models, tools, platforms and workflows designed to facilitate and expedite scientific research! Title: "Benchmarking Automated Scientific Enquiry: When AI co-scientists outpace peer review, what becomes the arbiter of truth?" Featured Speaker: Luca Foschini, PhD President & CEO, Sage Bionetworks Seminar 3-4pm, Networking Reception 4-5pm Share the Flyer! Bio: Luca Foschini, PhD, is President and CEO of Sage Bionetworks, a nonprofit that builds open infrastructure for biomedical data sharing, including the Synapse platform and community challenges such as DREAM. Before Sage he co-founded Evidation Health, where as Chief Data Scientist he spent over a decade leading research on wearable and real-world data for health. He holds a PhD in Computer Science from UC Santa Barbara, has published more than 70 peer-reviewed papers, and in a previous life represented Italy at the International Olympiad in Informatics. Abstract: In under two years, AI systems went from grade-school math to research-level problems, and the length of tasks an agent can complete reliably keeps doubling every few months. More than twenty AI co-scientists now promise to search the literature, generate hypotheses, analyze data and write up results. Do they reason like scientists? Recent evidence says not yet: agents often gather evidence and then ignore it, and better scaffolds barely help. The deeper problem is verification. AI moves fastest where answers can be checked instantly, as in code or proofs, while biology checks its claims at the pace of the wet lab and of peer review. I will walk through what works today, where these tools fail, and how benchmarks run as living community efforts, kept fresh and re-run on every new model, can keep us honest about what is still true., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform
